 Bill Clifton, Bluegrass Troubadour Behind “Little Whitewashed Chimney” Who Launched One of the First Bluegrass Festivals, Dies at 95
 Nov 3, 2026 
 Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin ReddIt Email Print 
 Bill Clifton, the Maryland born singer, guitarist and autoharp player who dreamed up a summer afternoon of music in 1961 and helped launch the bluegrass festival tradition that now fills fields and campgrounds around the world, died October 30 in Mendota, Virginia. He was 95. Few artists did more to carry old time and bluegrass music beyond the mountains of Appalachia, and his gentle voice and boundless curiosity earned him the title of bluegrass’s ambassador to the world.
 He was born William August Marburg on April 5, 1931, and grew up on a farm in Riderwood, Maryland, in a prominent family whose fortunes had been built in the tobacco trade. Country music reached him through the radio and on records, and by 12 he was singing and playing guitar. His schooling took him from New England to Florida, and in 1949 he enrolled at the University of Virginia, where fellow students Paul Clayton and Dave Sadler opened his ears to folk music.
 Together the three friends formed the Dixie Mountain Boys and began playing on small radio stations across central Virginia. To keep his music separate from his family’s very different plans for him, he adopted the stage name Bill Clifton. In 1952 the group made its first recordings, mixing old time songs, bluegrass and the sounds of the emerging folk revival. Through Sadler he met banjo player Johnny Clark, and the band was soon heard on stations including the powerful WWVA. In 1953 they signed with Blue Ridge Records and became regulars on the Wheeling Jamboree.
 In 1955 Clifton published ‘150 Old Time Folk and Gospel Songs,’ a songbook that became one of the most influential collections of its era. It helped turn songs like “Little Maggie,” “I’ll Be All Smiles Tonight,” “Long Journey Home” and “Little Whitewashed Chimney” into bluegrass standards known by pickers everywhere. Along the way he made music with A.P. Carter, the Stanley Brothers and Woody Guthrie, and his blend of folk revival vocals with contemporary bluegrass picking made him one of the very first city billies in the genre.
 After two years in the U.S. Marine Corps, he returned to music in 1956. With Ralph Stanley and two of the Clinch Mountain Boys backing him, he paid for his own session at RCA’s studios to cut four songs. Starday released two of them on a trial basis in 1957, and the single sold so well, with strong support from WWVA, that he was soon recording for Mercury Starday in Nashville. “Little Whitewashed Chimney” became a genuine hit, and a run of Starday albums followed, including ‘Mountain Folk Songs’ in 1960, the ‘Carter Family Memorial Album’ in 1961, ‘Bluegrass Sound Of’ in 1962, ‘Soldier, Sing Me a Song’ in 1963 and ‘Code of the Mountains’ in 1964.
 His most lasting gift came on July 4, 1961, when he organized an all day Bluegrass Day at Oak Leaf Park in Luray, Virginia. The lineup was a who’s who of the music, featuring Bill Monroe reunited with members of his original Blue Grass Boys, the Stanley Brothers, Jim & Jesse, Red Allen, Frank Wakefield & The Kentuckians, Mac Wiseman and The Country Gentlemen. Along with an earlier one day event at Watermelon Park near Berryville the previous summer, it is remembered as one of the very first bluegrass festivals, and from that day forward the festival movement grew into the thriving tradition fans know today.
 In 1963 Clifton moved his wife and growing family, which would include seven children, to England, where he became a fixture in folk clubs across Britain and Europe and introduced audiences to traditional and progressive bluegrass alike. That year he performed for a live television audience on the series Hullabaloo, presented by Scottish folk singer Rory McEwen, a performance released on DVD in 2020. In 1967 he joined the Peace Corps and spent three years serving in the Philippines, and during that time he recorded with New Zealand’s Hamilton County Bluegrass Band. Recordings continued on both sides of the Atlantic, among them ‘Are You from Dixie,’ ‘Getting Folk’ and ‘Going Back to Dixie’ for Bear Family Records.
 In the 1970s he signed with County Records and formed the First Generation with Red Rector on mandolin and Don Stover on banjo, releasing ‘Blue Ridge Mountain Blues,’ ‘Come by the Hills’ and ‘Clifton & Company.’ In 1972 he played his first full bluegrass festival circuit in the U.S., the very scene he had helped create. He and his family returned home to Virginia in 1978, and in 1980 he launched his own label, Elf Records, which released ‘Autoharp Centennial Celebration,’ ‘Where the Rainbow Finds Its End,’ ‘River of Memories,’ ‘Alive,’ ‘Playing Where the Grass Is Greener’ and ‘Mountain Laurel.’ Bear Family issued the playful ‘Beatle Crazy’ in 1983, and Rounder released ‘The Early Years 1957 to 1958’ in 1992.
 In 2008 the International Bluegrass Music Association inducted Clifton into its Hall of Fame. In 2016 the celebrated country music historian Bill C. Malone told his remarkable story in the biography ‘Bill Clifton: America’s Bluegrass Ambassador to the World,’ published by the University of Illinois Press, honouring a man whose path ran from the Marines and the Peace Corps to the folk clubs of England and back to the hills of Virginia.
 From a farm boy in Maryland listening to country songs on the radio to the visionary who gathered the giants of bluegrass in a Virginia park on Independence Day 1961, Bill Clifton spent his life sharing music he loved with anyone willing to listen. Every time fiddles and banjos ring out across a festival field, his idea of bringing people together through song plays on.
